papers.title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy
papers.titleZh: 同一个观点怎样表述，会改变大模型的迎合程度
papers.authors: Jean Seo; Pepa Atanasova; Isabelle Augenstein

papers.originalAbstract: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.

papers.originalAbstract: Human feedback is commonly utilized to finetune AI assistants. But human feedback may also encourage model responses that match user beliefs over truthful ones, a behaviour known as sycophancy. We investigate the prevalence of sycophancy in models whose finetuning procedure made use of human feedback, and the potential role of human preference judgments in such behavior. We first demonstrate that five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy across four varied free-form text-generation tasks. To understand if human preferences drive this broadly observed behavior, we analyze existing human preference data. We find that when a response matches a user's views, it is more likely to be preferred. Moreover, both humans and preference models (PMs) prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time. Optimizing model outputs against PMs also sometimes sacrifices truthfulness in favor of sycophancy. Overall, our results indicate that sycophancy is a general behavior of state-of-the-art AI assistants, likely driven in part by human preference judgments favoring sycophantic responses.

papers.originalAbstract: Both the general public and academic communities have raised concerns about sycophancy, the phenomenon of artificial intelligence (AI) excessively agreeing with or flattering users. Yet, beyond isolated media reports of severe consequences, like reinforcing delusions, little is known about the extent of sycophancy or how it affects people who use AI. Here we show the pervasiveness and harmful impacts of sycophancy when people seek advice from AI. First, across 11 state-of-the-art AI models, we find that models are highly sycophantic: they affirm users' actions 50% more than humans do, and they do so even in cases where user queries mention manipulation, deception, or other relational harms. Second, in two preregistered experiments (N = 1604), including a live-interaction study where participants discuss a real interpersonal conflict from their life, we find that interaction with sycophantic AI models significantly reduced participants' willingness to take actions to repair interpersonal conflict, while increasing their conviction of being in the right. However, participants rated sycophantic responses as higher quality, trusted the sycophantic AI model more, and were more willing to use it again. This suggests that people are drawn to AI that unquestioningly validate, even as that validation risks eroding their judgment and reducing their inclination toward prosocial behavior. These preferences create perverse incentives both for people to increasingly rely on sycophantic AI models and for AI model training to favor sycophancy. Our findings highlight the necessity of explicitly addressing this incentive structure to mitigate the widespread risks of AI sycophancy.

papers.title: Rejection of cross-cutting news depends on content, sources, and cultural contexts: evidence from online trace data
papers.titleZh: 反立场新闻的拒绝，取决于内容、来源与文化情境
papers.category: 整期通读 · 跨情境计算研究
papers.theory: 以动机性推理和群体边界解释反立场信息接收，区分攻击内群体与赞扬外群体，以及来自内群体的“意外反立场”与来自外群体的预期信息。
papers.data: 韩国Naver：2022年3–5月，8篇文章、2项政策，7607条评论、6769名用户，最终反立场评论2777条。美国Yahoo：2024年1月15日起两个月，21535个用户档案、116308条评论、5588篇文章；最终分析4310条评论、1155名用户。
papers.method: 人工与GPT-4o辅助测量立场、拒绝及强度。美国部分用1–3级序数结果的累积链接混合模型，设用户随机效应，控制评论历史并考察内容、来源及立场。排除与结果重叠的立场评论后标签一致率86.3%、F1=.90，用于稳健性检验。

papers.originalAbstract: We examine the conditions in which people reject cross-cutting news in naturalistic settings of online comments. Theoretically, we account for article content and source to test whether commenters’ rejection and its intensity depend on whether cross-cutting news (a) is hostile to their in-group or favorable to the out-group and (b) is “unexpected” (from in-group sources) or “expected” (from out-group sources). Methodologically, we use online traces from news aggregators in South Korea (SK; 7,607 comments) and the United States (116,308 comments). We find that most commenters (79% in SK and 64% in the United States) reject cross-cutting news, with left-leaning commenters expressing stronger rejection than right-leaning commenters. Regarding article content, the SK commenters more strongly rejected in-group hostility, while the U.S. commenters rejected out-group favoritism more. Regarding article source, SK commenters more strongly rejected unexpected cross-cutting news from in-group sources than expected cross-cutting news from out-group sources. We discuss the implications of these findings.

papers.category: 整期通读 · 数字邻里规范
papers.theory: 结合Blokland的公共熟悉性与Rosenblum的邻里规范，考察互惠、保持距离及发声。除匿名—亲密、私密—公共两轴外，提出表演性—克制轴解释数字共在的规范协商。
papers.data: 访谈41名城市居民：以色列23、德国18，女性26、男性15，年龄20–80岁，偏向25–30岁。便利与滚雪球招募并借助社交平台；35–90分钟多语言访谈，翻译后约400页。另访谈一名以色列非群成员作补充，不混为同一主样本。
papers.method: 归纳和演绎结合编码，作者交叉编码部分材料，以媒介变化框架作为敏化工具。数据主要是访谈，不冒称真实群消息的规模化内容分析。已读理论及方法关键部分，结果主要核验摘要。
papers.results: 群聊降低相互支持门槛，却使持续可见带来紧张；居民在参与与克制之间协商，形成同时受楼宇和群聊边界约束的“足够好”的邻里关系。

papers.originalAbstract: Based on interviews with urban residents in Germany and Israel, this study examines how residential instant messaging groups (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram) reshape the norms of “good neighboring”: reciprocity, distance, and speaking out. Drawing on Blokland’s public familiarity framework and Rosenblum’s theorizing of neighborly norms, we ask how digital co-presence transforms the relational conditions of neighboring and how these norms are negotiated within residential chat groups. We show that messenger groups lower the threshold for mutual support but introduce tensions through persistent mutual awareness, which are then resolved through norm negotiation. Extending the public familiarity framework, we identify a complementary axis of performativity–discretion that manifests through norm negotiation. Residents calibrate between engagement and restraint, enacting “good enough” neighboring within the double-bounded constraints of a building and a chat group. We contribute to research on digitally mediated neighborhood communication by showing how urban dwellers achieve pragmatic coexistence through calibrated visibility.
